opus-5.5.text:
I think world models address one of the most fundamental bottlenecks in embodied intelligence, and that bottleneck is data.

If you look at what happened with large language models, the key ingredient was the internet. Trillions of tokens of text were already sitting there, and we could train on them. For robots, we don't have that. There's no internet of robot actions. Every bit of physical interaction data has to be collected, usually through teleoperation, with real hardware, in real environments. That's slow, it's expensive, and it doesn't scale the way we need it to.

A world model is essentially a model that understands how the world evolves. You give it the current state, maybe some action, and it predicts what happens next. Once you have a model like that, it can help embodied AI in a few ways.

The first is synthetic data generation. If the world model is good enough, you can use it to generate a huge amount of realistic training data: different environments, different lighting, different objects, different scenarios that would be very hard or dangerous to collect in reality. Take autonomous driving. You can't go out and crash cars to collect edge cases, but you can simulate them with a world model.

The second is policy evaluation. Before you deploy a robot policy in the real world, you want to know whether it works. Testing on physical robots is time-consuming, and the results can be noisy. If you have a world model that can faithfully roll out what would happen when the policy acts, you can evaluate and compare policies much faster.

The third, and I think the most exciting longer term, is that the world model can become part of the robot's own intelligence. Humans do this all the time. Before you reach for a cup, you have some internal sense of what will happen. You imagine the outcome, you plan. A robot with a world model inside it can do the same thing. It can imagine the consequences of different actions and choose the better one. That's a path toward robots that reason about physics rather than just mimicking demonstrations.

That's part of the motivation behind our work on Cosmos at NVIDIA. We want to build world foundation models that developers can take and fine-tune for their own physical AI applications, whether it's robotics, autonomous vehicles, or something else. Not every company should have to train a world model from scratch. That costs enormous compute and data.

Of course, we're still early. Today's world models are impressive visually, but physical accuracy, long-horizon consistency, and how well they follow actions still need a lot of work. A video that looks plausible isn't the same as one that obeys physics. But I'm quite optimistic. I believe world models will play a role for physical AI similar to the one pre-training played for language models. They give you a foundation of understanding about the world that everything else can build on.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating data across varied environments and using world models to plan, but does not clearly say they help embodied intelligence perform well in settings beyond its training data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limited robot data and synthetic scenarios, but does not identify performing well beyond training data as a problem every AI system must solve.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it, a world model is basically a simulator that has learned the physics and the visual appearance of the world from data. And for embodied intelligence, whether that's a humanoid robot, a robot arm in a factory, or an autonomous vehicle, the biggest bottleneck right now is data. Large language models got to where they are because the internet gave them trillions of tokens of text. Robots don't have that. Every hour of real robot data is expensive, slow, and sometimes dangerous to collect. You can't crash a car a million times to learn what not to do.

So a world model gives you a few things. First, it's a data engine. If I have a model that understands how objects fall, how liquids pour, how a door swings when you push it, I can generate enormous amounts of realistic, physically plausible video of a robot doing tasks in many environments, many lighting conditions, many variations of objects. That becomes training data for the policy. We've seen this with Cosmos, where you can take a small amount of real demonstration and amplify it into something much larger and more diverse.

Second, it's a place to evaluate and plan. Before the robot acts, it can imagine. If I grab the cup this way, what happens? If I take this path, do I collide? That ability to roll the future forward in your head is what humans do constantly, and it's what makes us robust in situations we've never seen before. A world model is the component that gives a robot that same imagination.

And third, it closes the simulation gap. Traditional simulators are great for rigid bodies but they're hand-built, and they struggle with things like cloth, food, deformable objects, or just the sheer visual messiness of the real world. A learned world model can absorb that messiness directly from video. So you combine the two, the physics engine for ground truth and the world model for realism and coverage, and you get a training environment that is both correct and rich.

I'll be honest that we're early. Today's world models can still hallucinate, they can violate physics in subtle ways, and controllability is still a research problem. But the trajectory is very clear to me. The same scaling story that happened in language is starting to happen for the physical world, and embodied AI is going to be the main beneficiary.

r001.rationale: It says a world model lets a robot imagine outcomes and become robust in situations it has never seen, communicating that world models can help embodied intelligence generalize.

r002.rationale: It discusses limited robot data and handling unfamiliar situations, but does not identify performing beyond training data as a problem every AI system must solve.

astra-6.text:
I think world models can help embodied intelligence by giving an agent a way to anticipate the consequences of its actions. If a robot moves its arm or pushes an object, how will the world change? That prediction is useful because the robot can evaluate possible actions before executing them in the physical world.

But generating a visually convincing future is only part of the problem. For control, the model needs to capture the things that determine whether an action succeeds—contact, motion, and how objects interact. It also needs to account for uncertainty. If the robot cannot tell whether an object is stable, it may need to observe more or take a small, cautious action.

So I see world models as part of a loop: observe, predict, act, and then update based on what actually happened. They could make learning more efficient and reduce the amount of physical trial and error. The key is whether their predictions help an agent make better decisions in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting action outcomes and improving real-world decisions, but does not say world models help embodied intelligence generalize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models can give an embodied agent the ability to anticipate the consequences of its actions. When a robot reaches for an object, it needs to understand more than what is in the image. It needs to predict: If I move my hand this way, what will happen? Will the object move? Will I lose my grip?

A world model lets the agent explore those possibilities before acting. That could make learning more efficient, because physical interaction is slow and mistakes can be costly. The robot can learn from real experience, use the model to evaluate possible actions, and then check its predictions against what actually happens.

The challenge is making those predictions useful for control. A model might generate a very convincing video while getting the contact between a hand and an object wrong. For a robot, that small error can determine whether the task succeeds. So visual realism alone is not enough; we need action-conditioned predictions that capture the physical details relevant to the task.

I see world models as an important part of the system, together with perception, planning, and feedback. The agent should be able to imagine what might happen, act, observe the result, and adjust.

r001.rationale: The response says world models can predict action consequences and improve learning, but does not say they help embodied intelligence generalize.
